Talos.line: Villagers drift toward Talos with their worries; he answers each one plainly, the way a captain answers a scared recruit.
An old soldier working the ground straightens when Talos passes, and salutes without meaning to. Leadership is a thing people recognise on sight.
Talos walks the perimeter first, marking sight-lines and weak gates, then tells the elders exactly where to stand a watch.

Eleanor.line: Eleanor lays a hand on the shrine-stone and speaks the old blessing low, until the moss on it seems a shade greener.
Eleanor finds the local priest and they talk a long while — two people comparing notes on how a place keeps its faith when the dark presses in.
A grieving family sits apart from the others. Eleanor goes to them, sits in the dirt at their level, and simply stays.

Ragash.line: The children forget to be frightened the moment Ragash's hounds flop down in the square; soon a dozen small hands are buried in warm fur.
Local hunters fall in beside Ragash, asking — carefully, respectfully — how the hounds read a trail that they themselves keep losing.
Wild things settle when Ragash is near: a wary doe holds its ground, and a hawk circles once, low, as if reporting in.

Ronan.line: Ronan crouches at a smear of prints the others walked straight over. 'Three of them. Fast. Frightened, not hunting.' He is rarely wrong about this.
Something watches from the treeline and does not attack. Ronan lifts his chin a fraction; the Hidden Pack scouts acknowledge one of their own and melt away.
Ronan hangs back to speak quietly with Bram, voice pitched for a wolf and not a man. Whatever passes between them, Bram's hackles ease.

Torren.line: Torren runs a thumb along a cracked lintel and shakes his head. 'Whoever laid this was in a hurry. It'll come down in a hard winter.' Then he props it anyway.
Half the camp's tools are broken; Torren gathers them without being asked and works late, and by morning the axes bite true again.
Torren lingers over the old stonework, naming the joints and the tricks of it, half to the party and half to the long-dead hands that cut it.

Corwin.line: Corwin stops mid-stride, pulls out his journal, and sketches the thing everyone else was about to pass — 'for later,' he says, though later never seems to come.
Corwin kneels by the sick, weeping bark. 'This isn't rot. Rot is honest. This is being *made* to look like rot.' He notes it, unsettled.
Corwin points out a pale flower the others took for a weed. 'That only grows where the ground was salted with grief. Someone died here, and recently.'
Corwin reads the scuff-marks, the dropped strap, the way the door was barred from inside. He assembles the story the survivors were too frightened to tell.

Maeve Ashwood.line: Maeve is elbow-deep in someone's bad arm before the party has even set down their packs; she works fast, talks softly, and does not flinch.
Maeve seeks out whatever passes for a clinic here, restocks it from her own kit, and shows a shaking apprentice how to hold a needle steady.
Maeve checks the children first — always the children — pressing an ear to small chests and inventing a game out of every examination.
Maeve makes her quiet rounds of the old ones, warming stiff hands in hers, listening to complaints no one else has the patience to hear.
In the morning a satchel of clean bandages and fever-root is found on a doorstep. No note. Maeve says nothing, and no one has to ask.
